title: Best Qodo Alternatives in 2026
summary: Qodo alternatives compared on Git hosts, cost per review and comment noise: CodeRabbit, Cursor Bugbot, Gitar, Kodus, Greptile, Copilot and more.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Qodo has no permanent free plan, and its $30 Pro Team pack buys 2,000 credits, which Qodo puts at about 14 reviews, roughly $2.14 a review by our arithmetic.
- Four of the nine PR reviewers cover all four main Git hosts at general availability: CodeRabbit, Cursor Bugbot, Gitar and Kodus.
- Three review only on GitHub at general availability: GitHub Copilot code review (with Azure DevOps in public preview), Claude Code Review and cubic.
- Kodus is the only one of the nine you can self-host without a license fee; the others that self-host keep it on Enterprise.


Qodo alternatives are worth a look if your pull-request review bill has stopped being predictable. Qodo now meters reviews in credits on Pro Team, has no permanent free plan and pulled its IDE plugin on October 30, 2026, so there's more reason than usual to line up Qodo competitors.


Below are ten options, compared on Git hosts and how each one charges for a review. We checked every price on November 13, 2026.


Our own entry comes first because it's our product: we build[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) . The other nine are ordered by how many of the four main Git hosts (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps) each reviews on at general availability, widest first. Ties go alphabetically, a host in public preview breaks a tie upward, and the order implies no quality ranking.


## Why teams look past Qodo in 2026


Price is the first reason people compare. Qodo's FAQ says "We don't offer a permanent free tier", so after a 14-day trial with no card, you pay. The only free route left is a program for public GitHub repos with 200+ stars.


What you buy is credits. Pro Team is $30 for 2,000 credits, about 14 reviews a month by Qodo's sizing, and larger packs of 4,000 or 16,000 credits scale to about 29 or 114. The rate is $0.015 a credit, pooled across the team. Credits expire monthly, and overage bills at that rate up to a cap you set.


With a meter per review, your bill tracks how much the team ships, and billing is monthly only. Control features cost extra, as on most tools below: SSO/SAML, audit logs, BYOK, single-tenant and on-prem or air-gapped deployment all sit on custom-priced Enterprise.


The IDE plugin is the last reason: the tool once called Qodo Gen left VS Code, JetBrains and Visual Studio, though PR review is unaffected. AWS is ending its own editor plugin too, which is why teams are also weighing[Amazon Q Developer alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/amazon-q-developer-alternatives) .


None of this makes Qodo weak at review: it covers GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps Cloud and, on Enterprise, Gerrit, and it says "Qodo does not train models on your code." That host list is the bar for every entry below.


## The best Qodo alternatives, compared


All ten sit side by side below, ours in row one, with the Git hosts that set the order in the last column.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Four of the nine reviewers match Qodo on all four main hosts, one covers three, one covers two and three stop at GitHub at general availability.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Running work before review


**Overview:** Awesomic doesn't review pull requests, because we work a step earlier. Agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode) write the change on the project's own cloud computer, where they install and run real programs, so the code can run before anyone reviews it.


Several agents can work side by side, one chat apiece on the same files, and they carry on once your laptop is shut. Admins see every prompt and result and set approved models and budgets per person.


For a human check, hand a task from the same chat to a vetted developer on a separate expert plan, who takes it over or reviews the agents' work. We accept 0.82% of applicants and can match you in as little as 24 hours.


On data, none of the model providers behind our agents may train on your code, though our Terms let Awesomic train its own AI on de-identified content, and opting out works only from then on.


**Key features:**


- Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI models on one bill, or your existing Claude or Codex plan.
- More than 1,000 connected apps, including Slack and GitHub, plus your own MCP servers.
- A shared team keychain: add a key once and teammates' agents can use it with the value hidden.
- A browser app and desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux, plus iOS and Android apps.


**Pricing:** Pro is $199 per person per month, which is that person's monthly AI budget. The other three plans, Light at $19, Basic at $99 and Studio at $499, run the same agents and models, all billed monthly and non-refundable. A Dedicated expert is a separate plan, quoted on a call, with one Light seat included.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** Code can run before review, parallel agents, a vetted developer from the same chat, every prompt visible to admins


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Move the people who'll run agents onto Pro.
2. Open a project; a cloud computer comes with it.
3. Link GitHub from the app list, then store team keys in the keychain.
4. Give one agent a small task and let it run the code.
5. Ask for a Dedicated expert quote.


**Why it's a good Qodo alternative:** If your queue fills with changes nobody ran, our agents run the code they write before review.


**Final verdict:** Choose Awesomic to get code run before review, with an expert check on a separate plan. For comments inside your pull requests, CodeRabbit, Gitar or Kodus do the job we don't. If running the code first is what's missing,[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Pro.


### 2. CodeRabbit


**Overview:** CodeRabbit runs agentic reviews in the pull request, from a CLI and in your IDE. Its Learnings feature treats your replies as feedback for later reviews, and CodeRabbit never trains on customer code.


**Key features:**


- Pre-merge checks and 1-click fixes, so small findings close in the PR.
- Unit-test generation on Team and up.
- Triage, a prioritized PR queue, also on Team.


**Pricing:** Essentials is $24 per user per month billed annually, or $30 monthly, and Team is $48 annually or $60 monthly. Past the hourly allowance, each reviewed file costs $0.25, up to a cap an admin sets.


**Pros:** All four main hosts, seats only for PR authors, free forever on public repos


**Cons:** Essentials allows 5 PR reviews per developer per hour before metering, test generation needs Team, self-hosting is Enterprise only, for 500+ seats


**Why it's a good Qodo alternative:** It matches Qodo's four hosts with a seat price, metered per file only past the hourly cap.


**Final verdict:** Start here if your repos sit on more than one host.


### 3. Cursor Bugbot


**Overview:** Cursor Bugbot is Anysphere's reviewer, sold only inside Cursor plans from Premium up, which new customers buy as "The X Subscription" from X Subscription Corp. It covers all four main hosts plus self-managed editions and Cursor's Origin hosting, and it reads a PR's existing comments so it doesn't repeat them.


**Key features:**


- "Fix in Cursor" and Autofix, so a finding becomes an edit.
- Repo rules in` .cursor/BUGBOT.md` , org-wide ones in Bugbot Automations.
- A CI check on each PR.


**Pricing:** Premium is $30 a month, Super $100 and Ultra $200, or Teams at $30, $100 or $200 per seat by tier; Free and the $8 Plus plan exclude Bugbot. Its docs say "Bugbot uses usage-based billing" but give no per-review rate.


**Pros:** Wide host coverage, duplicate-aware comments, no training with Privacy Mode on


**Cons:** Needs a Cursor plan from Premium up, no published per-review rate, skips PRs above a default size, Bugbot API is Enterprise only


**Who gets the most from it:** Cursor users whose repos sit on self-managed hosts as well as cloud ones.


**Final verdict:** Pick Bugbot if Cursor is already your editor and an unpublished rate doesn't worry you.


### 4. Gitar


**Overview:** Gitar reviews pull requests, then works on the CI run behind them. Sonar acquired Gitar on May 21, 2026, and still sells it standalone. Gitar covers all four main hosts, plus Bitbucket Data Center and Azure DevOps Server. It keeps no source code, trains on none and holds zero-retention deals with its LLM providers.


**Key features:**


- PR summaries and high-signal review comments.
- CI failure diagnosis that separates broken code from flaky tests.
- A fix loop that runs until CI passes, on Pro and up.


**Pricing:** Core is $20 a user per month billed annually, or $25 monthly, and Pro is $40 annually or $50 monthly, both with unlimited repos. Open-source projects get Pro features free, and a 14-day trial needs no card.


**Pros:** Four main hosts, CI help beyond comments, no code retention


**Cons:** Fix loop, auto-approve and merge blocking need Pro, Core and Pro stop at 50 users, BYOK, SSO and self-managed GitLab need Enterprise


**What it adds over Qodo:** It treats a red CI run as part of the review.


**Final verdict:** Choose Gitar if flaky tests eat more review time than style comments do.


### 5. Kodus


**Overview:** Kodus calls itself "The open source alternative to CodeRabbit", with an AGPL-3.0 core plus a separate Kodus Enterprise license. You self-host it or let Kodus host it, on your own LLM key, and it reviews on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps and Forgejo or Gitea, self-managed editions included.


**Key features:**


- Plain-language Kody Rules, so a team convention becomes a check.
- Any OpenAI-compatible model endpoint, local ones included.
- CLI and CI/CD use outside the PR.


**Pricing:** Community is free, with unlimited PRs and users on your key, up to 10 rules and 3 plugins. Teams is $8 per developer per month billed annually, or $10 monthly, plus tokens paid to your provider at zero markup.


**Pros:** No license fee to self-host, self-managed Git hosts, local models


**Cons:** Token spend scales with PR volume, SSO, RBAC and audit logs are Enterprise, the AGPL and enterprise license split needs a legal read


**The case for it:** No other reviewer here runs on your own servers and model without a license fee.


**Final verdict:** Pick Kodus if you want to control the model and the hosting and can run it yourself.


### 6. Greptile


**Overview:** Greptile reviews with full-codebase context and charges per review rather than per seat. Cloud plans cover GitHub, GitLab.com and Bitbucket Cloud, with Cursor Origin in beta. Self-managed hosts, Gitea and Perforce are Enterprise only.


**Key features:**


- Plain-English rules plus learning from your team's PR comments.
- TREX, a sandbox agent that runs the PR branch to catch runtime bugs.
- Unlimited repos, even on the free Starter plan.


**Pricing:** Starter is free for 1 active developer with 50 credits a month. Pro has no seat fees and charges $1 per credit, where a base review costs 1 credit, a Plus review 3 and an Apex review 10, and a TREX run adds 3 credits on top.


**Pros:** No seat fees, runtime checks, free for qualified non-commercial OSI-licensed projects


**Cons:** No Azure DevOps, $1 to $10 per review by depth, the cloud may train on de-identified customer data unless an admin opts out


**Where it pulls ahead:** TREX runs your branch, so a review checks behavior as well as the diff.


**Final verdict:** Choose Greptile if PR volume swings month to month.


### 7. Sourcery


**Overview:** Sourcery sells "Perfectionist AI code review" with security scanning attached. It reviews on GitHub.com and GitLab, self-managed GitLab included on every plan, with GitHub Enterprise Server on Enterprise. Its docs list no Bitbucket or Azure DevOps, and it doesn't retain or train on your code.


**Key features:**


- PR summaries, inline comments and one-click fixes.
- Auto-approval of low-risk PRs under custom rules.
- Scans for secrets, SAST, IaC, dependencies and licenses, in full from Team up.


**Pricing:** Pro costs $12 a developer each month on annual billing, or $15 month to month, and Team is $24 annually or $30 monthly. Public repos are free, and Team has a 14-day trial with no card.


**Pros:** Low Pro seat price, self-managed GitLab on every plan


**Cons:** GitHub and GitLab only, Pro and free plans get only a security-scan preview, SSO and your own LLM keys need Enterprise


**Who it suits:** Teams on self-managed GitLab, which every Sourcery plan supports.


**Final verdict:** Try Sourcery for review and full security scans on one bill, at $24 a developer on Team billed annually.


### 8. GitHub Copilot code review


**Overview:** Copilot code review is GitHub's own reviewer, with Azure DevOps in public preview, and Copilot Free doesn't include it. GitHub's docs say that on re-review it "may repeat the same comments again, even if they have been dismissed."


**Key features:**


- Lite and Balanced effort levels, plus Max in public preview, so a typo fix doesn't pay for a deep review.
- Suggested changes applied in a couple of clicks.
- Suggestions handed to the Copilot cloud agent, in preview.


**Pricing:** Copilot Pro costs $10 a month, Pro+ $39 and Max $100, while Business is $19 per granted seat and Enterprise $39, and overage is $0.01 per AI credit. GitHub puts a review at about $0.25 on Lite, $1.50 on Balanced and $10 on Max on average, plus Actions minutes on private repos using GitHub-hosted runners.


**Pros:** Built into GitHub, cheap Lite reviews


**Cons:** GitHub only at general availability, repeated comments, no flat per-review price, no self-hosted option


**Why teams on GitHub pick it:** No new vendor if you already pay for Copilot.


**Final verdict:** Choose it if every repo lives on GitHub.


### 9. Claude Code Review


**Overview:** Claude Code Review is Anthropic's PR reviewer for GitHub, Enterprise Server included. Several agents hunt for issues in parallel, and a verification step filters false positives before anything posts. A review never approves or blocks a PR.


**Key features:**


- Inline findings ranked by severity.
- A summary and a check run on each PR.
- Average cost per review for each repo, shown to admins.


**Pricing:** It needs a Claude plan: Team costs $20 a seat a month paid yearly, or $25 paid monthly, for 2 to 150 seats, and Enterprise is $20 a seat billed annually plus API-rate usage, with a 20-seat minimum. Code Review "has no flat per-review price": token usage bills through usage credits, apart from the plan's included usage.


**Pros:** False-positive filtering, severity ranking


**Cons:** Team or Enterprise only, GitHub only, unavailable with Zero Data Retention or HIPAA configuration, spend varies with PR size and review frequency


**What sets it apart:** It aims its verification pass at the noise that makes teams dismiss AI comments.


**Final verdict:** Pick it if you're on Claude Team or Enterprise and GitHub.


### 10. cubic


**Overview:** cubic reviews each PR against your whole codebase and team rules, and gives it a merge-confidence score from 1 to 5. Its docs answer the host question bluntly: "Not yet. We currently only support GitHub."


**Key features:**


- Cross-repo checks for changes that break a neighbor.
- A set number of custom review agents on each plan.
- Policy-based auto-approval of low-risk PRs, with file globs it never approves.


**Pricing:** The free plan covers 20 AI reviews a month across the GitHub org. Team is $30 per developer per month billed yearly for 40k reviewed lines each, Pro is $79 for 80k and Max $160 for 160k.


**Pros:** Cross-repo awareness, custom agents, free for open-source teams


**Cons:** GitHub only, SOC 2 Type I, only the top 200 eligible files get reviewed on bigger PRs, SSO/SAML, audit logs and custom terms are Enterprise


**Worth a trial if:** A change in one service keeps breaking another.


**Final verdict:** Choose cubic for multi-repo GitHub codebases.

Qodo and the nine reviewers charge in seats, credits, tokens or a bundled plan, and each row gives a number to plan with.

Qodo Pro Team Pooled credit packs $30 for about 14 reviews, roughly $2.14 each by our arithmetic

Take 10 developers opening 100 PRs a month between them, assuming one review per PR. At Qodo's entry rate that's roughly $214 in credits. Seat tools at annual rates come to $240 for CodeRabbit Essentials, $200 for Gitar Core, $120 for Sourcery Pro, $300 for cubic Team and $80 plus tokens for Kodus Teams, while Claude Team seats cost $200 before review tokens.


Per-review pricing moves with depth: the same 100 PRs cost $100 on Greptile at base depth or $300 at Plus, and about $150 in Copilot credits at Balanced by GitHub's average, within the 19,000 credits pooled by 10 Business seats at $190, if review is their only use. Bugbot's Teams seats start at $300 before usage, and it reviews every PR update, so rerun the sum with your own PR and push counts.


Token billing is hardest to forecast, since Claude Code Review's spend depends on how big each PR is and how often reviews run, outside the plan's included usage. If Claude Code is on your shortlist beside the agents in[our Claude Code roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/claude-code-alternatives) , budget review separately.


## Signal versus noise in AI review comments


A cheap review means little if your team learns to ignore its comments. One field study shows how that plays out.


In[Automated Code Review In Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18531) , presented at ICSE 2025 SEIP per its arXiv record, Cihan and colleagues followed a bot built on the open-source Qodo PR-Agent with GPT-4 Turbo at Beko, on Azure DevOps. Of 4,335 PRs across three projects, 1,568 got automated reviews. Across 1,408 bot comments on merged PRs, 73.8% were labeled as resolved, and the study puts the Won't Fix share at 21.3%.


Average PR closure also rose, from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes. It's one company on an older setup, not today's Qodo, but it's a reason to time merges during your own trial.


In[a Google case study](https://sback.it/publications/icse2018seip.pdf) of about 9 million reviewed changes over two years, Sadowski and colleagues found a median latency under 4 hours for the whole review process, and the median change modified 24 lines. A separate five-week sample from 2016 put review time at an average of 3.2 hours a week per developer, the budget a noisy bot draws on.


The Google and Beko studies measure different things at different companies, so read each on its own rather than subtracting one from the other.


Users raise noise as a complaint, too. In an August 2026[r/codereview post](https://www.reddit.com/r/codereview/comments/1vssbl8/coderabbit_noise_is_seriously_getting_out_of_hand/) about CodeRabbit, the poster said big PRs get a wall of comments, many they'd never block on, so engineers learn to dismiss them and may skim the one that matters. That's one Reddit user's anecdote, but it's worth testing in any trial.


Whichever bot you pick, a person still reads what it posts. On a UI-heavy product, that reviewer helps most when they can judge the code and the screen it draws, which is one reason to[hire a design engineer](https://www.awesomic.com/design-engineer) rather than split review between a developer and a designer.


## Moving your review rules off Qodo


Switching reviewers is mostly a rules job, because a bot is only as quiet as the conventions you give it.


1. List the Qodo rules your team actually relies on, and drop any nobody has enforced in months.
2. Rewrite each in plain language for the new tool: Kody Rules in Kodus,` .cursor/BUGBOT.md` for Bugbot, plain-English rules in Greptile.
3. Run the new tool's trial on repos Qodo already reviews: 14 days for CodeRabbit, Gitar and Sourcery Team, 7 for cubic.
4. Count accepted and dismissed comments for each bot on the same PRs.
5. Cancel Qodo at the end of a billing month, since its credits expire monthly anyway.


Step 2 decides most of the quality. A rule that records a decision ("money values are integers in cents") beats vague taste. It's the same decide-first habit behind[design-driven development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/design-driven-development) , where the design is settled before the build starts.


## Tools we left off this list


A few names still show up in older roundups. PR-Agent, the open-source project Qodo started, is community-maintained under The-PR-Agent with an MIT license, and its GitHub description says it's "not the Qodo free tier".


Cursor's maker agreed to buy Graphite in December 2025, and Bugbot already has a slot. Ellipsis now pitches a managed agent platform with review as one use, and Bito leads with Governor, a model router, so we left both out.


## Mistakes to avoid when replacing Qodo


The first mistake is trialing on easy PRs. A reviewer quiet on a 20-line change may flood a 2,000-line one, and Bugbot and cubic both cap what they review on big PRs.


The second is reading "free" loosely. Free PR review on CodeRabbit and Sourcery covers public repos only, Greptile Starter covers 1 active developer, and Kodus Community still means paying your model provider.


The third is skipping data terms. Greptile's cloud can use de-identified customer data for training until an admin opts out, while Qodo, Gitar, Sourcery and CodeRabbit say they don't train on your code. Read ours too: our Terms let Awesomic use de-identified content to train its own AI until you opt out.


The last is expecting a code reviewer to catch visual bugs. Most code reviewers read the diff, not the screen, so a bot can flag a broken import and still miss a misaligned button. UI changes need a visual check before they merge, and[a design checklist](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/the-ultimate-design-checklist) is a place to start writing one.


## How to choose among Qodo alternatives


Start from your Git host, since it rules out the most Qodo alternatives fastest: the host table leaves four names on Azure DevOps, five on Bitbucket and six on GitLab.


Next, match the pricing unit to how your team ships. Steady PR volume suits a seat price on CodeRabbit, Gitar, Sourcery or cubic, and uneven volume suits per-review billing on Greptile, or on Copilot once you pay for the seat.


Ecosystem settles the rest. Bugbot only comes with Cursor plans from Premium up, so a team moving to one of the[Cursor alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/cursor-alternatives) loses its reviewer as well. Claude Code Review fits a company on Claude Team or Enterprise, and Copilot one already paying for Copilot. If Qodo's IDE plugin was the draw, CodeRabbit also runs in your IDE and writes unit tests on Team.


## Which Qodo alternative to trial first


First ask whether a bot is what's missing. If it's people, no reviewer will fix that, and an[unlimited development subscription](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/unlimited-development-subscription-why-is-it-worth-it-for-scaleups-and-enterprises) that puts a human developer on the work for a monthly fee fits better.


For a bot, pick two Qodo alternatives that review where your code lives, one seat-priced and one per-review, and run both on the same PRs for the seat-priced tool's trial (7 days on cubic, 35 reviews on Kodus Teams). Greptile Starter covers the per-review side for one developer, and Copilot means paying.


Keep the one whose comments your team resolves without stretching time to merge, and check its bill against the 100-PR sum above.


## FAQ


### What is the best free alternative to Qodo?


Kodus Community has no license fee for any number of PRs and users, though you pay your LLM provider for tokens. Greptile Starter covers one active developer and 50 monthly credits, and cubic's free plan gives 20 AI reviews a month. Public repos get CodeRabbit and Sourcery free, open-source projects get Gitar's Pro features, and Qodo's free program covers popular public GitHub repos, those with 200+ stars.


### Which Qodo competitors review pull requests on Azure DevOps?


CodeRabbit, Cursor Bugbot (on Azure DevOps Services), Gitar (including Azure DevOps Server) and Kodus all support it at general availability. GitHub Copilot code review supports Azure DevOps in public preview, and the other four don't.


### Does Qodo still have an IDE plugin?


No. The plugin formerly called Qodo Gen was retired from VS Code, JetBrains and Visual Studio on October 30, 2026. Qodo's pull-request review is unaffected, and its Agentic Toolbox now offers CLI skills for Claude Code, Codex and Kiro.


### How much does an AI code review cost per pull request?


Qodo's entry pack works out to roughly $2.14 a review by our arithmetic, Greptile charges $1 to $10 by depth, and Copilot reviews average about $0.25, $1.50 or $10 by effort level, drawn from a Copilot plan's AI credits. Seat-priced tools such as Gitar Core don't charge per review.


### Can I self-host an AI code reviewer?


Yes. You can run Kodus Community on your own servers with no license fee, paying only your model provider. Qodo, CodeRabbit, Greptile and Sourcery self-host only on their Enterprise plans, and GitHub Copilot code review has no self-hosted option.
